name: Cranial remolding helmet

lead: A cranial remolding helmet is a custom-fitted orthosis worn by infants with positional plagiocephaly, a flattened or asymmetric head shape, usually after repositioning has not helped. It is generally used between about 3 and 18 months of age.

The topic is relevant to appearance culture because head shape and facial symmetry are discussed there. Studies compare helmet and no-helmet groups, and Wikipedia describes high-quality evidence as lacking and use as controversial.

paras: The helmet is shaped to leave room where the skull is flat and contact where it is prominent, so that rapid infant skull growth fills the space and reduces asymmetry.

Wikipedia associates plagiocephaly with motor and language delays but states that this does not show plagiocephaly causes them. Insurers use measures like cephalic index to authorize helmets, and norms for that index have been questioned.

lead: A cranial remolding helmet, also called a cranial orthosis, is a custom helmet worn by infants to treat positional (deformational) plagiocephaly, in which the skull is flattened on one side or at the back. It is typically used between about 3 and 18 months of age after conservative care such as repositioning has not corrected the shape.[1]

Positional plagiocephaly became more common after back-sleeping guidance for preventing sudden infant death syndrome, and mild to moderate cases diagnosed before 4 months may respond to repositioning, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Whether helmets improve outcomes beyond natural improvement is debated. Wikipedia says high-quality evidence is lacking and that helmet use for positional cases is controversial.[1] A prospective non-randomized study of 128 infants compared helmet and no-helmet treatment.[2]
infobox: About 5 to 6 months for severe cases (Wikipedia)

paras: The helmet is made to an infant's head measurements and worn for much of the day. Severe cases are usually referred for a helmet, and Wikipedia says it works best when started at about 5 to 6 months.[1] Insurers commonly use the cephalic index (head width to length ratio) as one criterion for authorizing a helmet; a 2021 study updated cephalic index norms in a large diverse population because the older 1987 norms came from a small sample of white children.[3]
A prospective, non-randomized, longitudinal study of 128 infants (62 helmeted, 66 not) examined outcomes of both options, and a companion paper discusses the helmet-or-no-helmet decision.[2][4]
A study of 99 patients treated with helmet therapy used three-dimensional analysis to look at cranial and facial asymmetry, including mid-face prominence and ear position, after treatment.[5]
A 2023 systematic review analyzed conservative treatments, including helmets, for positional plagiocephaly in infants.[6]
No studies found on adult appearance outcomes.

Wikipedia reports an association between plagiocephaly and motor and language delays, adding that the link does not mean plagiocephaly causes the delay.[1] Prevention guidance cited there includes supervised tummy time and carrying the infant.[1]
Helmets are discussed in appearance-focused circles in connection with head shape and symmetry. The published studies concern infants with positional plagiocephaly.

timeline.event: Farkas and Munro cephalic index norms, later used by insurers, are established.[3]
Studies on helmet versus no helmet for positional plagiocephaly are published.[2][4]
Cephalic index norms are updated in a large, diverse population.[3]
Systematic review of conservative treatments for positional plagiocephaly.[6]
